AMAYO V. ERINMWINGBOVO (2000) LDLR-219(CA)

In The Court Of Appeal
(BENIN JUDICIAL DIVISION)
On Friday, the 19th day of May, 2000
Suit No: CA/B/260/96
Before Their Lordship
SUNDAY AKINOLA AKINTAN
Justice of the Court Of Appeal
RAPHAEL OLUFEMI ROWLAND
Justice of the Court Of Appeal
BABA ALKALI BA'ABA
Justice of the Court Of Appeal
BETWEEN 
OSAYEMWENRE APPELLANT 
AND
OSAYENDE ERINMWINGBOVO RESPONDENT 

JUDGMENT SUMMARY
INTRODUCTION:This appeal borders on ownership of land under Benin customary law.FACTS OF THE CASE:
This is an appeal against the decision of the Edo State High Court, Benin, delivered by Omage, J.
Respondent's case was that, his father was, until his death in 1950 the owner of a large farm situate at Ekoken in Orio Village in Benin Judicial Division. The respondent's father inherited the land from his father called Osagie who was the original founder and settler of the land in dispute. On the death of Osagie, the respondent's grandfather, the respondent's father as the eldest son inherited the land and planted rubber trees. When the respondent's father died in 1950, the respondent performed the burial customary ceremony rites and ceremonies and, in accordance with the Bini custom inherited the farm and the rubber plantation which he continued to farm. The respondent continued to farm on the land without any disturbance until sometime in 1959, when the appellant's father, one David Amayo, encroached on the rubber plantation. Respondent instituted an action against the appellant's father in the Grade 'A' Customary Court where the respondent obtained judgment. In 1979, the appellant, purportedly claiming through his father, broke into the farmland claiming part of it and commenced farming.

The plaintiff/respondent sued the defendant/appellant and claimed as follows:"1. Declaration that the plaintiff has possessory title to that piece of land situate at Orio village, Benin, within Benin Judicial Division and therefore the plaintiff is entitled to obtain a certificate of occupancy in respect of the land, shown on plan No. BEC 34.2. N1000. (One thousand Naira) damages for trespass on the said land in that in January, 1979, the defendant broke into the said land and started (sic) farming thereon without plaintiffs consent.3. An order of perpetual injunction restraining the defendant, his servants or agents from entering the said land without the plaintiff's authority."The appellant's case on the other hand is that the appellant as the eldest surviving son of his father buried his father in accordance with the Bini native law and custom.

It was the case of the appellant that the respondent, having sued and lost in a suit is estopped from bringing any action for declaration and trespass and injunction against the appellant as the matter is res judicata. Pleadings were filed and duly exchanged. After trial, the learned trial Judge found for the respondent, granting him all his claims with costs. Dissatisfied, appellant appealed to the Court of Appeal.
ISSUES:
The only issue submitted by the respondent for determination is:
"Whether the learned trial Judge was right in giving judgment to the plaintiff/respondent."
DECISION/HELD:In the final analysis, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the decision of the trial Court.


RATIO DECIDENDI

CUSTOMARY LAW - BENIN/BINI LAND TENURE SYSTEM - Procedure for acquisition of title to land under Bini customary law

"In Bello v. Eweka (1981) 1 SC 101 at pages 127-128, the Supreme Court had this to say: "Now, in Atiti Gold v. Beatrice Osaseren (supra), this Court approved the requirements of customary law for obtaining valid titles to native lands in Benin as set out by Idigbe, CJ (Mid-West State as he then was), from whose Court the appeal came to the Supreme Court in that case. The requirements as set out by the learned Chief Justice are as follows:- "A native may occupy land (i.e. any land not already in previous occupation of any individual) for farming purposes, and although such an 'occupier' is usually loosely referred to as an 'owner' he is not under Bini custom the legal owner until he has got the approval of the Oba of Benin to 'own' that land: this is because basically all land in Benin is owned by the community for whom the Oba of Benin holds the same in trust and, it is the Oba of Benin who can transfer to any individual the ownership of such land and until so transferred the occupier may continue to hold it for purposes of farming only. When therefore anyone wants or wished to own such land for purposes other than farming, i.e. of true ownership, that person must apply to the Oba through the plot allotment committee for ownership of it. It appears from the evidence that the procedure for obtaining complete ownership of such land by a non-occupier is this: the applicant must first negotiate with the occupier (usually farmer) to buy the occupier's interest (i.e. his crops) in the land and having settled with the occupier, he must then apply to the plot allotment committee who should satisfy that negotiation for transfer or purchase of the crops thereon has been settled thereafter." In Bello's case, the Court resolved a dispute of competing rights of parties who purchased the land from the same vendor and in doing so considered the issue of Oba's approval. The issue of title to land is different from the present case which is a case of inheritance based on the long possession or ownership by the respondent's family. In addition, the respondents claim was for possessory rights and the Court granted the respondent possessory right as claimed. With respect to the learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria, for the appellant, I am of the view that the case of Okeaya v. Aguebor (1970) 1 All NLR 8-9, setting out the procedure for acquiring title to land in Benin Kingdom is not applicable to the instant case in that title was acquired by the respondent's ancestors before 1961 before the setting up of the Allocation Committee, referred to in Okeaya (supra). In the instant case, the respondent cannot be regarded as an applicant for title to land who is required to submit an application to the Oba through the Allocation Committee as the land in dispute and the rubber plantation is a family property which has been in long possession of the respondent's family. As shown by the evidence before the trial Court, the respondent as the eldest son of his late father, having buried his father, inherited the farm and the rubber plantation. In other words, the farm and rubber plantation was originally owned by the grand-father then father of the respondent devolved on the respondent as the eldest male son of his father. I agree completely with the learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria that before a person can acquire title to land in Benin Kingdom, the approval of the Oba, must first be obtained. In my humble opinion the approval is only required in respect of new title to land through purchase or allocation but does not include land inherited such as in this case. We have not been referred to any authority which provides that the Oba's approval must be obtained before a person can inherit the property of his deceased parents. It should be noted that the title of the respondent's grandfather and father was never challenged by anybody."

Per BABA ALKALI BA'ABA ,JCA (Pp., paras.)




BABA ALKALI BA'ABA, J.C.A. (Delivering the Leading Judgment):

 The appellant who was the defendant in the trial High Court:- the Edo State High Court holding in Benin Judicial Division was sued by the respondent therein plaintiff, who claimed:-"1. Declaration that the plaintiff has possessory title to that piece of land situate at Orio village, Benin, within Benin Judicial Division and therefore the plaintiff is entitled to obtain a certificate of occupancy in respect of the land, shown on plan No. BEC 34.2. N1000. (One thousand Naira) damages for trespass on the said land in that in January, 1979, the defendant broke into the said land and started (sic) farming thereon without plaintiffs consent.3. An order of perpetual injunction restraining the defendant, his servants or agents from entering the said land without the plaintiff's authority."The facts of the case may be briefly stated as follows:-For the respondent, it is that his father was until his death in 1950 the owner of a large farm situate at Ekoken in Orio Village in Benin Judicial Division. The respondent's father inherited the land from his father called Osagie who was the original founder and settler of the land now in dispute. On the death of Osagie, the respondent's grandfather, the respondent's father as the eldest son inherited the land and planted rubber trees. When the respondent's father died in 1950; the respondent performed the burial customary ceremony rites and ceremonies and, in accordance with the Bini custom inherited the farm and the rubber plantation which he continued to farm. The respondent continued to farm on the land without any disturbance until sometime in 1959, which the appellant's father one David Amayo, encroached on the rubber plantation and trespassed on the land as a result of which the respondent instituted an action against the appellant's father in the Grade 'A' Customary Court where the respondent obtained judgment.In 1979, the appellant purportedly claiming through his father, broke into the farm land claiming part of it and commenced farming, hence the institution of an action against the appellant leading to this appeal. The appellant's case on the other hand is that the appellant as the eldest surviving son of his father buried his father in accordance with the Bini native law and custom. The appellant then inherited the land in dispute. It is the case of the appellant that the respondent, having sued and lost in suit No.B/64A/63 in the same subject matter as in this present suit by a Court of competent jurisdiction is estoppel from bringing any action for declaration and trespass and injunction against the appellant as the matter is res judicata.Pleadings having being ordered, filed and duly exchanged, the case went to trial before Omage, J., on the amended statement of claim to be found on pages 12-13 and Amended Statement of Defence at pages 14-15 of the record. The learned trial Judge, in a well considered judgment delivered on 27/7/98, found for the respondent granting him all his claims with costs.Being dissatisfied with the said judgment of the High Court, the appellant appealed by filing a notice of appeal containing the omnibus ground of appeal and subsequently with leave of this Court granted on 30/10/96 filed 2 additional grounds of appeal.Three issues were formulated in the appellant's brief as arising for our determination. They are:-1. Having regard to the totality of the evidence whether the learned trial Judge was right in giving judgment to the plaintiff/respondent.2. Whether the learned trial Judge was right in making use of Exhibit OE1 record of proceedings in a criminal proceeding in charge No.MB/113C/67.3. Having regard to the material and evidence before the Court whether the doctrine of estoppel per rem judicata avails the appellant.The only issue submitted by the respondent for our determination on the other hand states as follows:-1. Whether the learned trial Judge was right in giving judgment to the plaintiff/respondent.At the hearing of the appeal on 23/2/2000, learned counsel on either side each adopted his brief and expatiated thereon.In the appellant's brief of argument, Mr. A. O. Eghobamien, learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria, for the appellant, on issue No. 1, submitted that there is nothing on record to show that the respondent proved his case for a declaration of title under Bini native law and custom. Relying on the authorities of Okeaya-Inneh v. Aguebor (1970) 1 All NLR 1 at 8-9 and Aigbe v. Ogbeide (1998) 1 NWLR (Pt.557) 69 submitted that under Bini land tenure system, title to all lands in Benin Kingdom was vested in the Oba of Benin as a trustee for the people and that all others held mere possessory title based on the "approval" granted by the Oba. Learned Senior Advocate further submitted that it is trite law that in a claim of declaration of title, the onus is on the plaintiff to prove his case and that the plaintiff must rely on the strength of his case and not on the weakness of the defendant's case.On issue No.2, Learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria for the appellant referred to several pages of the record, contending that the learned trial Judge relied heavily on Exhibit OE1 in his judgment. Learned Senior Counsel contended that the result of a criminal case can not be used to establish a civil claim. Arguing issue No.3, learned Senior Advocate for the appellant, referred to Paragraphs 8 and 9 of the Amended Statement of Claim and Paragraphs 4 and 6 of the Amended Statement of Defence and submitted that the plaintiff did not lead evidence to prove his claim contained in Paragraphs 8 and 9. In conclusion, he urged us to allow the appeal.In reply, Dr. Onaghise, Esq., submitted in the respondent's brief that the respondent as plaintiff had proved his case and the judgment in his favour is good judgment which is unassailable. Learned Counsel for the respondent submitted that the certified copy of proceedings of the criminal case is admissible and that it is not correct to say that the learned trial Judge relied on the copy of the proceedings Exhibit OE1 only in reaching his decision. He pointed that it is clear from Exhibit OE1 that the dispute between the respondent and the appellant's father for which the respondent was charged before the Magistrate Court was in respect of dispute over rubber plantation, and Exhibit "OE1 and OE4" are used to determine the use of estoppel per rem judicata.Learned Counsel explained that the claim of the respondent was not "for title", simpliciter but for possessory right over his late father's rubber plantation. He finally, urged us to dismiss the appeal and affirm the judgment of the trial Court.Having studied all the issues formulated by the parties in this appeal, it appears to me that the sole issue formulated by the respondent has adequately encompassed all the issues and it is for that reason that I intend to determine the appeal on the said issue herein reproduced.I will start by reproducing the portion of the judgment of the learned trial Judge at pages 39-41 of the record which has attracted my attention as it is my humble opinion relevant in resolving the sole issue. "The defendant's counsel has submitted that the testimony of the plaintiff as to the inheritance and acquisition of the land does not conform to known procedure for acquisition of land in Benin outskirts before 1960. He said the correct procedure is to plant an Ikhimwin tree after obtaining approval or right to the land from the Oba of Benin. In this suit the plaintiffs claim to the root of title relates back to 1950s, it is not in dispute that the claim is made prior to the introduction of ward system in Benin. It may be the practice to plant an Ikhimwin tree to identify the area of land claimed by the ancestor of the plaintiff; there is no contradiction of the evidence that the plaintiff's ancestor deforested the area of Ekoken, Orio where the land resides. I therefore accept the testimony of the plaintiff as it is unchallenged. See Ikhuomela v. Oniwaja (1990) 4 NWLR (pt.146) 617. From the testimony of Osagiede in Exhibit OE1, the predecessor in title of the defendant had made a claim to a wrong plantation.Evidence shows that the plaintiff through his predecessors in title had been in long continuous uninterrupted succession to the parcel of land now in dispute, the onus is on the defendant to dislodge the claim of the plaintiff by cogent evidence. See Rickets v. Shote (1960) L.L.R. 201; and Makinmi v. Ladejobi (1960) LLR. 233. In this case no cogent evidence has been adduced by the defendants to dislodge the claim of the plaintiff to the land. Specifically on Benin land tenure, the plaintiff has shown a good title to the land than the defendant; This claim is better than that of the defendant. In Atiti Gold v. Beatrice Osaseren (1990) 1 All NLR 125 at 134. Coker, J.S.C. observed as follows: which observation I respectfully adopt."The question at all times was which of the parties had made a good title to the land and certainly not which of them first obtained the Oba's approval."In the instant case neither of the parties is possessed of Oba's approval. By the testimony of the plaintiff he has proved a long continuous uninterrupted succession to the land. In the case of the defendant even the claim to the land through the plantation derived from the root of the plaintiffs claim to the land. In many respects the facts of this case are not dissimilar to those in Arase v. Arase reported in 1981 5, Supreme Court, where Idigbe, J.S.C. as he then was adopted the reasoning in Gold v. Osareren (supra), and held that the proof of a better title to the land in dispute is sufficient to ground a right to a declaration to possession over the land. This is so in spite of the fact that the particular procedure for grant of the land by the Oba of Benin had not been followed by the plaintiff. In the instant case, evidence shows that the plaintiff's predecessor in title deforested the land in dispute and was the Enogie of the Area in Orio where the lands reside. No evidence was given that he planted Ikhimwin tree, or that he obtained the consent of the Oba of Benin in 1953, before he surveyed the land. Evidence however, shows that at no time was the predecessor in title of plaintiff challenged on the ownership of the plantation or land. The defendant has produced no evidence of continuous use of the land, and such evidence of claim to plantation that he tendered derived its root from the ancestor of the plaintiff: even the identity of the plantation is uncertain. I have no hesitation in holding therefore that the plaintiff has produced a better evidence of long continuous uninterrupted possession to the land in dispute, and I have no hesitation in awarding to him a right to possessory title to that land situate at Orio village Benin: as contained in Exhibit OE1 tendered in these proceedings. The plaintiff claims also the sum of one thousand Naira damages for trespass to the said land. Trespass under our law is a tort which by decided authorities is described as unjustifiable intrusion by one person upon the land in possession of another. Ngwo v. Onyejena (1964) 1 All NLR 352. In Oyadeji v. Adenle (1993) 9 NWLR (pt.316) 224 the definition of trespass in England v. Palmer (1955) 1 WACA 659, where trespass was defined as the invasion of one, be it ever so minute into the land of another, without the consent of the later; and it is actionable per se. The defendant has averred that he has possession of the land; through his ancestor. There is no direct evidence of the entry of the defendant himself into the land. I am not unmindful of the testimony in Exhibit O.E.2 in which Osagiede Erinmwingbovo the brother of the plaintiff said in the lower Court in the Exhibit that the father of the defendant David Amayo, had gone unto a different plantation from the one he sold to him; and that he did not sell the plaintiffs plantation to the defendant's father with admission by the father of the defendant that he was on plaintiffs plantation; trespass is clearly established to David Amayo. Trespass however is not committed vicariously. It is a personal right which accrues to the person in possession of the land upon a wrongful entry to the land by a person who enters the land wrongfully. The present defendant cannot be adjudged to, be liable for that trespass. I do not therefore so find on those grounds. The plaintiff has however testified that the present defendant has testified that the defendant himself, and with his servants and agents have and entered the land in 1979, and while therein drove away plaintiff workers on the land, and proceeded to plant crops on the land. The averment was never denied by the defendant. I have no reason not to allow, and admit as true such unchallenged evidence. I therefore admit it as evidence of trespass by the defendant to the land in dispute. Upon this holding, I find the defendant liable for trespass to the land and award against him the sum of One thousand Naira (N1,000.00) for trespass in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff claim also for an order of injunction which I hereby allow as follows:"An order of perpetual INJUNCTION TO RESTRAIN the defendant; his servants or agents from entering the said land, at Ekoken Orio village, Benin City the area and admission of which are shown in Exhibit O.E.1 in this suit, In sum the plaintiff has succeeded in his claim in this suit; and that is the judgment of the Court."As can be seen from the portion of the judgment quoted above, the learned trial Judge in my humble opinion properly considered the case of the parties. It is a case where the case of one party has weight while the other has no weight at all. In my view, the learned trial Judge was right in his conclusion as the only witness, the mother of the appellant was unable to give any credible evidence particularly regarding the source of ownership of the land in dispute other than asserting that the land belonged to her late husband and it was inherited by his son, the appellant. In Bello v. Eweka (1981) 1 SC 101 at pages 127-128, the Supreme Court had this to say: "Now, in Atiti Gold v. Beatrice Osaseren (supra), this Court approved the requirements of customary law for obtaining valid titles to native lands in Benin as set out by Idigbe, CJ (Mid-West State as he then was), from whose Court the appeal came to the Supreme Court in that case. The requirements as set out by the learned Chief Justice are as follows:-"A native may occupy land (i.e. any land not already in previous occupation of any individual) for farming purposes, and although such an 'occupier' is usually loosely referred to as an 'owner' he is not under Bini custom the legal owner until he has got the approval of the Oba of Benin to 'own' that land: this is because basically all land in Benin is owned by the community for whom the Oba of Benin holds the same in trust and, it is the Oba of Benin who can transfer to any individual the ownership of such land and until so transferred the occupier may continue to hold it for purposes of farming only. When therefore anyone wants or wished to own such land for purposes other than farming, i.e. of true ownership, that person must apply to the Oba through the plot allotment committee for ownership of it. It appears from the evidence that the procedure for obtaining complete ownership of such land by a non-occupier is this:the applicant must first negotiate with the occupier (usually farmer) to buy the occupier's interest (i.e. his crops) in the land and having settled with the occupier, he must then apply to the plot allotment committee who should satisfy that negotiation for transfer or purchase of the crops thereon has been settled thereafter."In Bello's case , the Court resolved a dispute of competing rights of parties who purchased the land from the same vendor and in doing so considered the issue of Oba's approval. The issue of title to land is different from the present case which is a case of inheritance based on the long possession or ownership by the respondent's family. In addition, the respondents claim was for possessory rights and the Court granted the respondent possessory right as claimed.With respect to the learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria, for the appellant, I am of the view that the case of Okeaya v. Aguebor (1970) 1 All NLR 8-9, setting out the procedure for acquiring title to land in Benin Kingdom is not applicable to the instant case in that title was acquired by the respondent's ancestors before 1961 before the setting up of the Allocation Committee, referred to in Okeaya (supra).In the instant case, the respondent cannot be regarded as an applicant for title to land who is required to submit an application to the Oba through the Allocation Committee as the land in dispute and the rubber plantation is a family property which has been in long possession of the respondent's family. As shown by the evidence before the trial Court, the respondent as the eldest son of his late father, having buried his father, inherited the farm and the rubber plantation. In other words, the farm and rubber plantation was originally owned by the grand-father then father of the respondent devolved on the respondent as the eldest male son of his father. I agree completely with the learned Senior Advocate of Nigeria that before a person can acquire title to land in Benin Kingdom, the approval of the Oba, must first be obtained. In my humble opinion the approval is only required in respect of new title to land through purchase or allocation but does not include land inherited such as in this case. We have not been referred to any authority which provides that the Oba's approval must be obtained before a person can inherit the property of his deceased parents.It should be noted that the title of the respondent's grandfather and father was never challenged by anybody . I therefore resolved the sole issue against the appellant. In the result, having regard to the foregoing, the appeal fails and is hereby dismissed. I affirm the judgment of the learned trial Judge, Omage J., delivered on 2717/95. I award costs assessed at N3,000.00 in favour of the appellant. 

SUNDAY AKINOLA AKINTAN, J.C.A. :

 I agree.

RAPHAEL OLUFEMI ROWLAND, J.C.A. :

 I had the privilege of reading in advance the judgment just delivered by my learned brother

Ba'aba  J.C.A. The facts are well set out and the lone issue was fully considered. I therefore have nothing useful to add. I agree with the judgment. The appeal lacks merit and it is therefore dismissed. I endorse the order on costs.Appeal dismissed.
